This board workshop presentation, "Secondary Classroom Tech Vision 2022," outlines the Troy School District's plan to extend its classroom technology model from elementary to secondary schools. It was presented at the March 1, 2022 Board of Education Workshop.

The Big Why: The district frames its goal as a learning experience that is mobile, wireless, flexible, collaborative, cohesive, and equitable.

2021 recap: The Elementary Classroom Refresh equipped rooms with a new 86-inch TV along with a 2020 MacBook M1 Air, a document camera, an Apple TV, and a movable cart. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Business Office memorandum dated March 2, 2022 from Rick West to the Board of Education, outlining proposed updates to the District's Policy Manual for consideration at the March 15, 2022 Regular Meeting. The revisions were recommended jointly by Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board of Education Policy Committee, and District Administration, and the memo explains each contemplated change organized by section of the Policy Manual. The Business Office is at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098.

Introduction: No recommended updates.

Bylaws - Policy 1000.02, Meeting of the Board of Education: The memo modifies the quorum provision and removes the Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation section. It notes that the Michigan Open Meetings Act (OMA) underwent significant revision after the onset of the pandemic - after initially allowing broad latitude for online meetings and remote participation, those options were significantly scaled back in OMA revisions that took effect January 1, 2022. Removing the section still permits remote participation in limited situations as provided in the OMA. On quorum, unless otherwise required or permitted by law, a majority of serving members constitutes a quorum; a member not physically present at a duly held meeting where a quorum is already present may participate remotely by telephone, teleconference, video conference, or other electronic means so long as any attendee can hear and interact with them, and must notify the presiding chair 24 hours in advance; such a member may vote to the extent allowed by Michigan law. For meetings where members attend remotely, the Board Secretary must name each remote member in the minutes, the remote member must hear and be heard, the member must notify the Board President at least one business day before the meeting so the public can be told how to contact them, and the Board President must ensure the public knows how remote members voted, such as through roll-call voting.

Students - Policy 2000.01, Admission and Enrollment (Children of Non-resident Employees): Prior language is revised so that a child of a non-resident District employee may enroll without paying tuition only if enrolling in the K-12 program, not some other District offering. Once enrolled, the student may continue to attend through graduation or receipt of a certificate of completion, though the policy does not bar long-term suspension or expulsion for a Student Code of Conduct violation.

Students - Policy 2000.02, Learning Environment (Child Find): Consistent with state and federal law on supports and services for students with disabilities, districts must have policies to identify and locate every resident student who may have a disability. The recommended 'Child Find' language commits the School District to attempt to identify and locate every student residing in the District who may be a student with a disability under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An internal memorandum from the Troy School District Technology Services department (4420 Livernois; phone 248.823.5060), dated February 23, 2022. The memo is from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, and concerns the Secondary Classroom Display and Audio project.

The memo transmits an attached recommendation letter from Convergent Technology Partners supporting the award of the secondary classroom technology work. Soggs explains that the district will use the RFP issued in April 2021 (Bid Number 9925) that was originally used for the elementary classrooms. Because that bid pricing is valid for one year and the district has been satisfied with both the products and the vendor's performance, staff concluded that using this existing contract award is in the district's best interest rather than re-bidding.

The revised scope of work includes: removal and disposal of the existing Smartboard/Projector; removal and disposal of the existing classroom audio (speakers, amplifier, and microphone) at the middle schools; purchase and installation of an 86" TV, a TV wall mount, and all necessary HDMI, audio, and power cables; and soundbars for the middle school classrooms. The soundbar pricing is drawn from the competitive PEPPM contract (contract number 529461-006), because soundbars were not included in the elementary classroom project. High school classrooms will instead reuse their recently installed amplifiers and speakers, with the vendor connecting the new TVs to the existing classroom audio.

The overall scope covers upgrades for 250 secondary classrooms and 115 soundbars. A 10% contingency of $68,600 has been added to cover additional materials that may be needed to reinforce walls, to add smaller TVs in other small instructional spaces, and to add technology to new instructional spaces that may or may not be added in the fall of 2022.

Staff seek Board approval to award the secondary classroom display and audio project to InaCOMP TSG for a total project cost, including the contingency, of $865,715. The memo states this project will be funded from the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. It corresponds to agenda item 8.A at the March 15, 2022 Regular Meeting of the Board of Education.

The Executive Summary frames a strategic initiative to "Enhance Security and Visibility" and pairs three desired outcomes with Arctic Wolf's solution: (1) operationalize a full-feature SIEM that leverages existing IT and security controls, correlates environmental telemetry, and provides detection and response; (2) deliver a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service to provide visibility, monitoring, response, and remediation of security events and incidents; and (3) provide a service-based solution that identifies, evaluates, and gives quarantine and remediation guidance for threat indicators in real time. Stated business risks include revenue/operational risk from a cyber attack, distraction of already-burdened IT staff by reactive response, and undetected dormant vulnerabilities. A slide presentation on the Troy School District English Language Arts Curriculum Review and Revision for Grades 9-12, covering the 2021-2022 effort and shown at the April 5, 2022 Board of Education Workshop.

The deck opens with collectively developed priorities: the need to effectively serve all students; attention to recent SAT college-level reading readiness data; addressing the gap between high- and low-performing students; adequate teacher training for advancing readers; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

Supporting data show a decrease in SAT College Level Reading Readiness across two cohorts. Cohort 1 (2016-2018) posted 9th grade 82.47, 10th grade 83.50, and 11th grade 76.85, a decrease of 5.62%. Cohort 2 (2017-2019) posted 9th grade 86.80, 10th grade 84.70, and 11th grade 81.44, a decrease of 5.36%. The presentation quotes Michael Fullan et al.'s Breakthrough (2006) on schools' need to get all students to meet high standards and become lifelong learners as low-skilled jobs shrink from roughly 95% of jobs two decades earlier to about 10% of the economy.

The proposed shift moves from the current 'limited options, linear path' (9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, 12 Lit and Comp, alongside an honors track of 9-10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, 12 AP Literature) to a 'preferred' model with more options and all students prepared for choice: a revised 9th Grade English (2023-2024) and 10th Grade English (2024-2025) leading to American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and electives. The rationale draws on the Michigan Common Core State Standards' capacities of the literate individual (demonstrate independence, build strong content knowledge, respond to varying demands, comprehend and critique, value evidence, use technology and media strategically, and understand other perspectives and cultures).

Much of the deck describes extending the elementary and middle school 'workshop' (WS) model into high school, aligning literacy instruction from 5th and 6th grade upward. Lessons learned from the middle school workshop include keeping the student at the center, foregrounding skills over content, offering choice in reading and writing, prioritizing practice time, and normalizing in-the-moment feedback. Middle school teachers reported reluctant readers reading more, students writing more (jots, long and flash drafts), and deeper engagement, while identifying growth areas in conferring and small-group resources and professional development.

Ongoing teacher support is detailed: 5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021; 8 in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021; 11 in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021; a full day of teacher-led PD in August; and on-site days with Teachers College, including Staff Developer Natalie Louis working with coaches and secondary administrators in early 2022. Ninth-grade teachers and coaches continued visiting middle school classrooms.

The current work centers on a 9th-Grade Curriculum Development Team (CDT) that prioritized skills and outlined skills for all six units, with the goal of writing six workshop-style, skill-based units to be piloted in 2022-2023, and a plan for the CDT to observe middle school classrooms through the lens of the three workshop commitments.

What it is
Informational slide deck, 'Cybersecurity in K12,' presented at the April 5, 2022 Board of Education Workshop.

Why K-12 is targeted
- Schools tend to under-invest in IT support and security and run older, out-of-date systems due to budget constraints.
- As essential community services, districts face pressure to pay to restore operations, increasing extortion leverage.
- Children's Social Security numbers are especially valuable because they are unused and unmonitored, enabling 'synthetic ID' fraud (illustrated with a Frank Abagnale quote and the Anthem breach).

Incident examples
- Baltimore County Public Schools (MD), 115,000 students: attack detected 11/24/20; classes canceled ~3 days.
- Huntsville City Schools (AL), 23,000 students: early dismissal 11/30/20; students reverted to pencil and paper.
- Toledo Public Schools: student/employee names and SSNs leaked online; spent $75,000+ and provided identity/credit monitoring.
- Richmond Community Schools (MI): malware found 12/27/19, entered via the district's heating/cooling service provider, affecting heating, phones, copiers, and classroom tech; $10K bitcoin ransom declined; school closed Jan 2-3.
- Walled Lake School District (MI): confirmed hack; engaged forensic and cyber-counterintelligence experts under a cyber-security insurance policy.

Troy School District's own experience
- Ransomware attacked file shares via a phishing link early in the era of such attacks; it spread through much of the central office network, but files were recovered from backups within a week and data was only encrypted, not exfiltrated.

Other content
- References the K12 cyber incident map (k12cybersecure.com) and insurance compliance considerations.

Purpose
Raises Board awareness of K-12 cyber risk and the District's exposure and response.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An informational slide presentation titled 'Cybersecurity in K12,' delivered at the April 5, 2022 Board of Education Workshop to raise awareness of the threats facing school districts.

The deck first explains why K-12 districts are targeted: schools usually under-invest in IT support and security, their computer systems tend to be older and out-of-date because of budget issues, and because schools are essential to their communities a shutdown gives attackers greater leverage to extort payment. It stresses that children's Social Security information is far more valuable than an adult's - a minor's number is typically pristine, unused, and unmonitored, so a criminal can combine it with another name, address, and birth date to create a 'synthetic ID' for fraud. The point is underscored with a Frank Abagnale quote that fraudsters will always take the child over the adult, and a reference to the Anthem breach.

Several real incidents are summarized. Baltimore County Public Schools in Maryland (115,000 students) detected an attack on Tuesday, 11/24/20 before Thanksgiving, canceling classes about three days before resuming 12/2/20 and affecting computers, the district website, email, remote learning, the grading system, and school offices. Huntsville City School District in Alabama (23,000 students) had an early dismissal on 11/30/20 and reverted students to pencil and paper. Toledo Public Schools had names and Social Security numbers of current and former students and employees leaked online, spent more than $75,000 on cybersecurity experts, and provided identity theft and credit monitoring for everyone whose files were stolen. Richmond Community Schools discovered malware on 12/27/19 that entered through the district's heating and cooling service provider and affected critical systems including heating, phones, copiers, and classroom technology; the district faced a $10,000 bitcoin ransom, declined to pay, and closed school on January 2nd and 3rd. Walled Lake School District confirmed its systems were hacked, with an official (Gutman) noting the district engaged forensic experts, a cyber-counterintelligence consulting firm, and a specialist law firm under its cyber-security insurance policy and alerted authorities.

The presentation then turns to Troy School District's own experience: ransomware attacked the District's file shares through a phishing link when such attacks were in their infancy, quickly spreading through much of the central office network files. People named: The proposal was presented to Beth Soggs (IT Director) and Alan Wilson (Network Manager) of Troy Schools, and prepared by Nick Hankins (Account Executive) and Chris Pittman (Sr. Systems Engineer) of Arctic Wolf, with Bryan Teipel (President) and Dave Benham (Solution Architect) also listed under 'People Driven.'

Structure: The proposal is organized into six sections—Executive Summary, Current Assessment, Why Arctic Wolf, Security Risk Quantification, Pricing Proposal, and Partnership and Enablement.

Executive Summary: The strategic initiative is to 'Enhance Security and Visibility.' Desired outcomes include operationalizing a full-feature SIEM that leverages existing IT and security controls and correlates environmental telemetry; a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service to provide visibility, monitoring, response, and remediation of all security events and incidents; and a service-based solution that can identify, evaluate, quarantine, and provide remediation guidance for threat indicators in real time. Current Assessment: The proposal describes Troy Schools as having a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to a central hub, making environment-wide visibility a challenge; multiple security tools in place but limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts; and a lack of a broad detection-and-response mechanism. It states IT and security resources are constrained, that the cost and complexity to build a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is 'probably unrealistic,' and that the district has expressed interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic 'alert-response' services. Business risks cited include revenue/operational risk from cyber attack, distraction of already-burdened IT staff by reactive response, and the danger of dormant vulnerabilities enabling larger and longer-term breaches.

Value drivers described include 'Benchmark Your Business' (revealing configuration gaps and digital risks that vulnerability tools cannot identify), 'Team Enhancement' (adding named security operations experts), 'Faster Intrusion Detection' (using the existing technology stack without rip-and-replace), and 'Harden Your Environment' (a Concierge Security Team, or CST, evaluating vulnerability and risk data, presenting on-demand executive reports and personalized remediation plans, then validating that open vulnerabilities have been closed). Under service offerings, 'Managed Risk' is described as designed to prevent incidents, citing the Center for Internet Security's finding that 80% of breaches could have been prevented if the organization had met the top 5 CIS controls. The extracted text is truncated before the detailed pricing proposal, though the companion memo lists the first-year cost as $156,140.48.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: “Survey on a Potential Bond Proposal, April 2022” presents the results of a public-opinion poll conducted by EPIC MRA of Lansing, Michigan (4710 W. Saginaw Hwy., Suite 2C), for the Troy School District Board. Methodology: 400 live operator telephone interviews were completed March 20 through March 24, 2022, with a margin of error of +/- 4.9 points; 74% of interviews were completed via cell phone. Respondents were included only if residency was confirmed within Troy School District boundaries, they had demonstrated 2018 November election vote history (or were previously too young to vote), and they indicated they would at least probably, if not definitely, vote in the November 2022 general election. Respondents were given detailed information about the district’s future capital needs. For the 2-mill proposal, they were told a $525 million proposal could be funded, with tax implications of about $200 more per year—just under $17 more per month—for every $200,000 in market value and $100,000 in taxable value of a home. The 2-mill proposal drew 66% total YES support. Among the N=263 YES respondents, the top open-ended reasons were that infrastructure/facility improvements are needed to stay modern (23%), being pro-education/always voting yes (17%), having or knowing children who would benefit (11%), preserving the district’s world-class reputation (8%), for the children/future (6%), and maintaining property values (6%). Among the N=108 NO respondents, the top reasons were a tax increase/taxes too high/cannot afford it (34%), wasteful spending/distrust/lack of transparency (18%), improvements not needed (10%), too much money at once (7%), and teachers underpaid/should raise teacher pay instead (5%). Respondents who opposed the 2-mill proposal were then asked about a scaled-back $420 million, 1-mill proposal, with tax implications of about $100 per year (just under $9 per month); combined with prior YES votes, the 1-mill proposal reached 79% total YES. Those still opposed were asked about a further scaled-back $295 million, 0-mill proposal, which would not require any increase above current millage levels but would renew the existing millage dedicated for Troy Schools for a period of 30 years; combined with prior YES votes, it reached 84% total YES. A final “Vote Progression” slide restates the 66% total YES figure for the initial 2-mill ask.

Additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor was expected by June 1.

The letter details major features of the proposed budget. Social-Emotional Wellbeing and Mental Health Support: in response to increased pandemic-driven need, Oakland Schools shifted resources by adding two mental health consultants, using these positions to broaden mental-health worker support in schools under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act, and deepening professional learning through programs such as Youth Mental Health First Aid and Trauma-Informed Instruction. Career and Technical Education: to align with the Michigan Department of Education's "Top 10 in 10 Years" goals, additional resources are dedicated to CTE, including the four technical campuses and operational funding for the CTE mobile classroom (the STEMi), which became operational in spring 2021; having increased the CTE allocation to local education agencies (LEAs) by more than 25% in 2019-20, Oakland Schools continues that funding level in 2022-23. Shared Services: Oakland Schools provides technology, business office, instruction, and truancy services on a cost-recovery basis; technology services are provided to sixteen constituent districts, and business office services to four districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA). MiPEER Consortium: in FY 2012-13, Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts formed the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MiPEER) to select a countywide Enterprise Resource Planning system for human-resources and financial applications, standardizing the Chart of Accounts and business processes and converting to PowerSchool BusinessPlus in phases between 2015-16 and 2022-23. Illuminate: Oakland Schools has contracted with Illuminate Education as its county-wide student assessment and data-analysis vendor since Fall 2016, with all twenty-eight districts and two public school academies covered by the license; the Oakland Schools Board of Education agreed to provide a 50% subsidy for the Illuminate DnA assessment software and support in 2022-23, with add-on "Item Banks" available at districts' cost.
